After twenty years of sitting on the other side of the table, I can tell you that a board asks the same three questions about any number, in the same order. The first is: is this comparable? Like for like, with the one-offs stripped out, is this the same thing we looked at last quarter? If you have not answered that before you are asked, the rest of your slide does not get heard. The second question is: is it going to happen again? People forgive a one-off. What they do not forgive is a one-off that turns up three quarters in a row wearing a different name. And the third question is the dangerous one, because everybody prepares the first two and forgets this one. What are you doing about it? And please, do not tell me you are monitoring it. Monitoring is not a fix. When a board hears we are monitoring the situation, what it hears is: no answer yet.

I use the passive voice all day long and I am not embarrassed about it. When the pipeline was not updated, the person who did not update it is not the information. Naming them in a board meeting moves everybody's attention to a person instead of a problem, and the problem is what we are there to solve. But there is a line, and the line is this. When the agent is you, say so. If it was my decision, I say I decided. The moment I say it was decided, everyone in that room starts hunting for the author, and they find me anyway, only now it looks like I tried to hide. The other half of the rule matters just as much. Good news always takes the active voice. Somebody built that result, and if I say the result was achieved, I have quietly stolen it from them. So: the passive for the problem, my own name for my own decisions, and their names for anything that went right. What a board is really testing is not the number. It is whether you know which parts of it are yours.
